## §04 — The word looks around

`5:01` → `6:33` · 13 beats · 193 words · 93s · `04-the-word-looks-around.md`

> No storyboard yet — `npm run check:board`.

| at | say | on screen |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `5:01` | So every "dog" starts out identical. Which can't be right — and it isn't, for long. |  |
| `5:08` | Because a token never stays on its own. It's sitting in a sentence. |  |
| `5:15` | And before anything else happens, every token gets to look at the others. | the full sentence, all rows visible |
| `5:21` | Here's what looking means. Our token asks every other token one question: how much do you matter to me? | lines from our token to the rest |
| `5:30` | Some matter a lot. Most barely matter at all. | the lines thicken and thin |
| `5:35` | And it can only look backwards — at the words already there. Not at what's coming. |  |
| `5:42` | Then it takes a bit of each one, in proportion, and mixes it into itself. |  |
| `5:49` | And its row changes. Same token. New numbers. | the row visibly shifts |
| `5:54` | That's attention. That's the whole idea — every token adjusting itself based on the company it's in. |  |
| `6:02` | Now watch why that matters. "The dog barked." And "a hot dog." | two sentences, side by side |
| `6:08` | Same word both times. Started as the exact same row. Ended up nothing like each other. | both rows, clearly different |
| `6:15` | So the numbers don't belong to the word any more. They belong to the word in this sentence. |  |
| `6:24` | And notice — none of that could have been worked out ahead of time. It depends entirely on what you typed. |  |

| at | say | on screen |

| `13:23` | You run it again. |  |
| `13:26` | The word it just made gets added onto the end of your sentence. | the new word joins the end of the sentence |
| `13:32` | And the whole thing goes back in. From the beginning. |  |
| `13:37` | New sentence — one word longer. Forty-five floors. Look around, pick experts, do the work. | the stack runs again |
| `13:44` | And another word comes out. |  |
| `13:47` | Then again. And again. One word at a time, until it decides to stop. | the loop, accelerating |

| `14:01` | Every single word of that reply. Full stack. Fresh choices. |  |
| `14:06` | So it isn't three hundred and thirty-six choices. It's three hundred and thirty-six per token, per word it writes. It never stops choosing. |  |

## §12 — How people actually run these

`15:40` → `17:33` · 14 beats · 236 words · 113s · `12-how-people-actually-run-these.md`

> No storyboard yet — `npm run check:board`.

| at | say | on screen |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `15:40` | Except — people do run models like this on small machines. Right now. And they're not lying about it. |  |
| `15:49` | So what are they doing that we just failed to do? |  |
| `15:55` | Caching. | one word on screen |
| `15:57` | Here's the thing we noticed all the way back at the start. Experts repeat. Not always — but often enough to matter. |  |
| `16:07` | The next token quite often wants some of the same experts the last one did. | a couple stay lit between two words |
| `16:14` | So you don't fetch every time. You keep the ones that keep coming back in fast memory, and you only go to the drive for the ones you're missing. |  |
| `16:27` | And it works. Genuinely. On a model with eight experts on each floor, a small cache catches most of what you need. | the cache filling |
| `16:37` | Which turns the whole thing into one question. How much do you keep close? | a slider appears |
| `16:44` | Keep more, and it's fast — but now you need a big machine again, which is the thing we were trying to avoid. | dragging up |
| `16:55` | Keep less, the machine gets small — and the misses pile up, and it crawls. | dragging down |
| `17:02` | And remember what we're choosing from. Two hundred and eighty-eight experts, on each of forty-two floors. |  |
| `17:09` | Twelve thousand and ninety-six slots. | the number builds |
| `17:12` | There's no setting on that slider where it's both. That's the trade, and on a model chopped this fine the exchange rate is brutal. |  |
| `17:23` | So you can run it on less. It'll just be slow. That was never a wall — it's a price. |  |

## §13 — What that number actually bought

`17:33` → `19:16` · 12 beats · 220 words · 103s · `13-what-that-number-bought.md`

> No storyboard yet — `npm run check:board`.

| at | say | on screen |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `17:33` | So. Eighteen billion active. |  |
| `17:35` | Here's what that number is actually telling you. |  |
| `17:40` | Per word, this thing does the thinking of a model about a twentieth of its size. That's real. That's why it's quick, and why it's cheap to run per word. That part is completely true. | the work bar, small |
| `17:55` | But all of it still has to be within reach. Because it never knows which part it wants until the moment it wants it. | the whole model, heavy |
| `18:06` | So: "active parameters" is a compute number. It was never a memory number. |  |
| `18:13` | Sparse routing buys you compute. It doesn't buy you memory. | both, side by side |
| `18:18` | And here's the part I didn't expect. This model has a hundred and twenty billion parameters, and it fits on one chip. This one has three hundred and twenty, and needs four. | two models appear |
| `18:32` | Both of them use about five percent of themselves to answer you. |  |
| `18:38` | The difference is that this one is chopped finer. More experts, smaller each. |  |
| `18:44` | Which is exactly why it's better — and exactly why it's harder to hold. |  |
| `18:51` | So the better these models get at using less of themselves, the more of them you have to keep lying around. |  |
| `19:01` | A three-hundred-and-twenty-billion-parameter model doing eighteen billion of work is still a three-hundred-and-twenty-billion-parameter model. It just isn't a three-hundred-and-twenty-billion-parameter bill. And that's the difference between something that's cheap to run — and something that's small. |  |
